book: 074 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike

chapters.file: ch26 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Michael Ruse reads the 1968 film as a study in forbidden knowledge: Dr. Zaius has sealed the cave of human artifacts because he knows a prior human civilization destroyed itself and fears the knowledge could cause a repetition. Weighing nuclear weapons, recombinant DNA, bird-flu research, and data-driven political manipulation, Ruse argues Zaius's censorship is both impossible and undesirable, since the search for knowledge is intrinsically valuable and containment only increases the need for research. The film's deeper lesson is evolutionary: intelligence and sociality co-evolved only to the level 'good enough,' so any species that acquires weapons of mass destruction will likely destroy itself, meaning the Planet of the Apes scenario would recur across the universe.

chapters.file: ch27 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch28 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Lori Gruen uses Taylor's cage and Caesar's confinement in Rise to examine real chimpanzee captivity in research labs and sanctuaries, asking whether captivity wrongs apes even when it causes no physical or psychological suffering. Against the view that autonomy requires language-grade self-endorsement, she argues chimpanzees are autonomous: they make choices, deceive (Tristan's false alarm call among the vervets), follow social norms, and set things right (Sheba returning Sarah's book), so denying them freedom is itself a wrong, as Caesar's 'Am I a pet?' moment shows. Since wild habitat is vanishing, she concludes the best we can do is captive care that respects apes' wild dignity and lets them come as close to feeling at home as captivity allows.

chapters.file: ch29 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: John Wilkins treats Caesar, who spares the neighbor he has beaten, as a Kantian exemplar whose reason lets him adopt the Categorical Imperative, contrasting him with the rational egoism of the film's human keepers and executives. He argues the film trades on the outdated Great Chain of Being, which Darwinian tree thinking dissolves: with no higher or lower species, only branching homologies, human nature must be continuous with ape nature, and talk of innate species essences must allow for statistical variation and dispositions rather than determination. Caesar's morality also needs more than reason, namely the primate dispositions of deference and empathy scaffolded by his human family, though Buck's instant moral conversion after enhancement shows the film is ambivalent about whether scaffolding alone explains it.

chapters.file: ch30 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch31 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: John Huss asks whether Andy Serkis deserved an Oscar nomination for playing Caesar through performance capture, and argues that 'What is acting?' is a Socratic-style definitional question (like stumping Euthyphro on piety) of the sort Wittgenstein diagnosed as a language confusion, since the definition of movie acting is in flux. Using the seeing-as debate, Kuhnian theory-ladenness of observation versus Fodor's Muller-Lyer point that belief does not dictate sight, he explains why animators and fans see such different things in the identical raw footage. He concludes, with James Franco, that acting is an emergent ensemble property of actors reacting to one another on a shared stage, which performance capture enables rather than threatens, and a coda notes PETA's hope that CG performers will end the use of animal actors.

chapters.file: ch32 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Tom McBride reads the film through Wittgenstein's On Certainty: Dr. Zaius's certainties (flight is impossible, humans come from the forests) are hinge or riverbed propositions that cannot be doubted within the ape form of life, so Taylor's true story sounds not false but insane, like claiming to have slept on the moon. Speaking and able to prompt empirical investigation, Taylor fractures a foundational principle where G.E. Moore, facing a 'wild tribe' playing a different language game, could only confess that things 'stand fast' with him; and Zaius's explicit origin myth, a parallel to Plato's Myth of the Metals, is flimsy precisely because rulers who must insist on rules are not potent and are reduced to destroying the cave evidence. The genre's appeal is Margaret Atwood's 'controlled hallucination': crazy doors that swing on safe hinges, rivers that still have stable beds.

chapters.file: ch33 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.

chapters.file: ch34 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch35 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Chad Timm reads Caesar's arc, from 'Am I a pet?' to 'What is Caesar?', through Lacan: the mirror stage fixes an alienating ideal-I (his reflection, the human children he watches), entry into sign language inducts him into the symbolic Other, and the over-stuffed signifier 'pet' confronts him with the real, precipitating an identity crisis that deepens when the shelter chimps also reject him. Against Descartes's cogito, an unconscious structured like language means the self can never fully know itself, and Zizek's ideological fantasy explains how the new master signifier Freedom quilts Caesar's ape liberation, with humans cast as the savage oppressive Other. His closing 'Caesar is home' completes the Zizekian Act, traversing the ideological fantasy and retroactively redefining the coordinates of his identity.

chapters.file: ch36 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jason Davis opens with Sammy Davis Jr. thanking the white producers for the best film ever made on black-white relations, and their cluelessness, to show that white privilege rests on an epistemology of ignorance, paralleled by the human enjoyment of ape slavery in Conquest. He reads the ape castes through the ontology of race: the films first stage race as biological realism and essentialism (warrior gorillas, chimpanzee scientists, orangutan priests), but Battle for the Planet of the Apes shows biology is not destiny, and human genetics (race accounts for about 0.012 percent of human variation) discredits biological racial realism altogether. Via Charles Mills's social ontology of race and Kwame Anthony Appiah's racial skepticism, the chapter treats ape racism as a mirror of anti-miscegenation-era America whose racial categories are social constructs, down to the dropped ape-human hybrid child.

chapters.file: ch37 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Shaun May uses Heidegger's being-in-the-world to mark off the human: Caesar correcting Charles's fork grip shows a grasp of the unspoken norms governing equipment, and the apes of the 1968 film, surgeons with scalpels and years of training, inhabit the same world of projects, skills, and tools that Heidegger says other animals lack. Language seals the difference: Taylor's syntax, Zaius's carefully ordered 'The Almighty created the ape in his own image,' and socially learned practices like pointing and map-reading stand against Nim Chimpsky's syntax-free signing and chimps' failure to understand pointing. Caesar's foresight in stealing the ALZ-113 before leading the escape extends this to Heideggerian temporality, and the ape uprising becomes a move toward authenticity, lives owned as a meaningful narrative whole.

chapters.file: ch38 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
ch39 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Norva Lo and Andrew Brennan set Richard Routley's 'last man' thought experiment beside Taylor's triggering of the doomsday bomb in Beneath the Planet of the Apes: both ask whether wiping out every living thing would be wrong once no humans remain to be harmed, which basic human chauvinism cannot condemn. The chapter argues the act is wrong from both sides: non-anthropocentrism counts the apes, mutants, and horses as intrinsically valuable beings, and even human-centered standards condemn it, since the talking apes and mutants are Locke's rational persons and Nova's people are biologically human, making Taylor's outburst 'you damned dirty ape' a form of speciesism. Taylor emerges not as simply mad or evil but as the Cold War logic of mutually assured destruction made flesh, a warning that excessive self-interest, personal or species-level, is itself the danger.

chapters.file: ch40 - Planet of the Apes and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Eugene Halton retells human history as the fable of Peirce's 'degenerate monkey': a neotenous, instinct-weak blunderer (Homo errans) whose gift for abductive guessing and attunement to the intelligence of the wild was inverted by agriculture and civilization into Narcissistic self-mirroring, anthropocentric religion, and the worship of the machine. The telepathic, rubber-masked mutants of Beneath the Planet of the Apes who worship the Alpha-Omega bomb ('I reveal my Inmost Self unto my God!') become a prophecy of our own screen-mediated, empathy-poor life, from Facebook to Botox, in Huxley's pleasure-conditioning rather than Orwell's pain. Against this, the chapter holds up Armando's Franciscan empathy for Caesar and the hope of a 'planet of the regenerate monkeys' re-attuned to the community of wild life.

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of common descent and the branching evolutionary tree replaced linear, ranked pictures of the living world.
holes.why: Chapter 29 builds its whole argument on Darwin's tree (against the Great Chain) to deny any pinnacle species and to place human nature in continuity with ape nature.

holes.name: The Great Chain of Being
holes.what: The pre-Darwinian idea, named by Lovejoy, that all living things are ranked on a single linear scale from simple to complex with rational humans at the top.
holes.why: Chapter 29 argues the Ape films assume this chain view of grades and that Darwinian tree thinking dissolves it, undercutting 'higher' and 'lower' species and species essences.

holes.name: Semiotics (the theory of signs)
holes.what: The Peirce-Saussure theory that meaning is carried by signs whose content comes from convention, association, and interpretation rather than inherent properties.
holes.why: Chapter 33's core claim is that Goldsmith's score means nothing inherently and works only through learned sign-associations, an argument that needs the missing semiotics vocabulary.

holes.name: Jacques Lacan
holes.what: French psychoanalytic philosopher who rethought the self through the mirror stage, the imaginary-symbolic-real registers, and an unconscious structured like language.
holes.why: Chapter 35 reads Caesar's entire identity crisis through the mirror stage, the ideal-I, meconnaissance, and the three registers, none of which any existing taxonomy entry covers.

holes.name: The Mirror Stage
holes.what: Lacan's account of how the infant's jubilant identification with its mirror image founds an alienating ideal-I and a lifelong misrecognized sense of self.
holes.why: Chapter 35 applies the mirror stage directly to Caesar's reflections and to the human children he identifies with as the origin of his identity crisis.

holes.name: Slavoj Zizek
holes.what: Lacanian-Marxist philosopher of ideology who analyzes how ideological fantasy structures social reality and how an Act can change the coordinates of the possible.
holes.why: Chapter 35 leans on Zizek's The Sublime Object of Ideology for ideological fantasy, the traumatic kernel of the real, and the Act that Caesar performs at the film's end.

holes.name: Ideological Fantasy and the Act
holes.what: Zizek's notion that fantasy quilts social reality around a master signifier, hiding a traumatic lack, and that traversing the fantasy through an Act redefines one's identity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses ideological fantasy to explain Caesar's new master signifier Freedom and his ape liberation, and the Act to read his final 'Caesar is home'.
